draft.title: Hybrid functions and modelling
card: A hybrid (piecewise) function uses different rules on different parts of its domain. Each rule is written with the x-values it applies to.
Example: a taxi charges $3 per km up to 10 km, then $2 per km after that. For x ≤ 10, C(x) = 3x. For x > 10, C(x) = 30 + 2(x − 10).
To find a value, first check which x-interval the input is in. Then use only that rule. For x = 14, use the second rule: C(14) = 30 + 2 × 4 = 38.
If the pieces meet at the boundary, the graph has no jump there. Here 3 × 10 = 30 and the second rule also gives 30 at x = 10, so the graph joins up.
draft.remember: Pick the rule by the interval the input falls in, then use only that rule.

a.q: A function is f(x) = 2x + 1 for x < 3, and f(x) = 10 − x for x ≥ 3. What is f(5)?
a.why: Since 5 ≥ 3, use the second rule: f(5) = 10 − 5 = 5. The first rule gives 11, but it only applies for x < 3.
a.clue: Check which interval 5 is in first.

b.q: Mia's gym charges C(x) = 20x dollars for x ≤ 8 visits, and C(x) = 160 + 12(x − 8) for x > 8. What is the cost for 11 visits?
b.why: Since 11 > 8, use the second rule: 160 + 12 × 3 = 160 + 36 = 196. The tempting $220 applies 20 to every visit, but the cheaper rate applies only after 8 visits.
b.clue: Only the visits after the 8th use the second rate, and 160 is the cost of the first 8.
